newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton wants action on gases, toxic waste.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants action on gases, toxic waste.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday issued a sweeping environment statement, calling for legally binding commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and the reduction of toxic wastes and deforestation.

"We share a responsibility to preserve a future for our children and grandchildren, we must care for our shared environment," Clinton said in a speech under a blazing sun in a seaside park on Australia's tropical northeast coast.
"It is a practical and moral imperative," he said.
"We are citizens of not only individual nations but this small and fragile planet," Clinton said.
Clinton used the backdrop of the aqua-blue Pacific Ocean and Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, to deliver his plea to save the world's environment.

"I call upon the community of nations to agree to legally binding commitments to fight climate change. "We must stand together against the threat of global warming," said Clinton, who is on a five-day visit to Australia.

"A greenhouse may be a good place to raise plants, but it is no place to nurture our children. And we can avoid dangerous global warming if we begin today and if we begin together," he said. "We must work to reduce harmful greenhouse gas emissions."
He said the 1987 Montreal Protocol had slowed production and consumption of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), the "chemicals which have been eating a hole in the earth's ozone layer".
"We are on our way to closing the ozone hole...now we must see to it that this landmark treaty is enforced from one corner of the earth to another," Clinton said.

"These gases released by cars and power plants and burning forests...are literally warming our planet. If they continue unabated the consequences will be nothing short of devastating for the children here in this audience and their children."
The international community agreed in Montreal in 1987 to phase out production of CFCs and some other ozone-depleting substances. The Montreal Protocol was signed by 150 governments.
CFCs, widely used in refrigerants and elsewhere in industry, deplete the ozone layer through a chemical reaction. The ozone layer filters out harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun.
Clinton's call for legally binding commitments to reduce greenhouse gases was in contrast to the U.S. stance at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 when Washington avoided such a position.
He also called for a reduction in global toxic waste.
"Toxic chemicals and pesticides found here and in the United States can still find their way into our lives, endangering our lives, our lands and our children," Clinton said.
"Let us now forge a global agreement to stop these toxic substances from being released into the world around us."
Clinton also called on the United Nations to develop a strategy for sustainable forest management, saying deforestation was clearing an area the size of South Korea annually.
He said protection of the environment and economic growth were compatible and that enviromental destruction contributed to conflict, citing the troubles in drought-striken Africa.
Clinton praised Australia's efforts to protect the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system with 2,600 reefs linked for 2,500 kilometres (1,550 miles) along the coast.
"We must be allies in the 21st century to protect the earth's environment," Clinton said.
Environment Minister Robert Hill, also at Port Douglas, urged Clinton to work for a permanent global whaling ban.

"We urge the United States to take a moratorium against whaling to a permanent ban on whaling," said Hill in introducing Clinton. "If we can achieve that Mr President, civilised society will have taken a step forward," Hill said.
Japan and Norway refuse to agree to a permanent ban on whaling, citing scientific or indigenous reasons.
Clinton later went to the Great Barrier Reef some 30 miles offshore to swim and snorkel. Earlier, he and his wife Hillary visited a rainforest reserve and fed and patted kangaroos.
Clinton also craddled a nine-month-old koala named after his daughter Chelsea. "She is beautiful," said a smiling Clinton.
He flies to Manila on Saturday for next week's APEC summit.
